palette.notes: Author's advice: limit beginners to about 5 colours until shading and clusters are solid; minimal palettes stayed central to his style. Number is the article's recommendation, not a measurement.

lighting: Minimal palettes are credited with improving lighting and shading control; pillow shading is named as a beginner mistake.
silhouette: Style rests on repeated choices: one projection (his 1/2 side view), recurring subjects and consistent cluster shapes; outlined clusters show how little detail can still carry character.

motion.timing: Not covered; notes that large sprites look impressive but take much longer to animate and can feel clunky.

texture: Simple, repeated clusters feel clean or cute; varied spontaneous clusters feel sketchy or organic. Avoid duplicate stray pixels and too many colours.
camera: A single consistent projection (1/2 side view, abstract over realistic perspective) is a style signature.

acting.acts: Staging lesson: a fixed set of constraints (palette, projection, subject) makes every scene recognisable as the same world.
acting.depth: Not covered; abstract flat projection preferred over realistic perspective.

techniques: limit the palette (about 5 colours) until shading is solid
avoid pillow shading: shade from a light direction, not from the outline inward
pick one projection and keep it (1/2 side view)
consistent cluster language: simple repeated clusters for a clean, cute look
small expressive sprites over large sprites that are slow to animate
feel: few colours + one projection + repeated clean clusters = a recognisable world from the first frame
for_fred: Lock Fred and Pixie's style rules (palette count, outline rule, side-view projection, sprite size) in one spec and reuse them in every reel; keep the sprites small enough that adding a new act (exit, return, background cameo) is cheap to animate rather than adding more effects.
